# Research

My current research develops the **Sources of Uncertainty** framework for Bayesian inference and explores its applications. The framework draws inspiration from decision-theoretic ideas about uncertainty.


## Sources of Uncertainty

Bayesian inference represents uncertainty through subjective probability distributions. The **Sources of Uncertainty** framework starts from the observation that the researcher may have different degrees of confidence in different parts of this probabilistic specification.

The framework incorporates this distinction by associating each component of a factorized prior with a confidence parameter. This allows the researcher to specify not only prior beliefs, but also the degree of confidence assigned to each source of uncertainty.

The confidence mechanism operates differently from standard prior informativeness, providing a new modelling lever and greater flexibility in how the posterior is shaped.


## Sparse Bayesian learning

Building on the Sources of Uncertainty framework, I propose **SoU-SGL**, a sparsity-inducing Bayesian method based on global-local prior structures.

While standard global-local priors mainly induce shrinkage, SoU-SGL uses source-specific confidence to push irrelevant components more sharply toward zero.


## Bayesian neural networks

I apply these ideas to Bayesian neural networks, using structured sparsity to recover compact architectures.

In current work on convolutional neural networks, the procedure identifies compact architectures with similar total size and layer-wise allocation across different starting widths. These architectures maintain competitive accuracy with standard deterministic neural networks while improving probabilistic performance.

# Research

My research develops methodological tools for Bayesian inference and Bayesian machine learning. The central object in my current work is the **Sources of Uncertainty** framework, together with its applications to sparse Bayesian learning and Bayesian neural networks.

Motivated by ideas from decision theory, this work treats confidence as an explicit modelling ingredient in Bayesian inference. The goal is to give researchers additional ways to design Bayesian models and control how information from data and prior components shapes the posterior.

## Sources of Uncertainty

I develop the **Sources of Uncertainty** framework, which extends Bayesian inference by assigning confidence parameters to different components of a probabilistic model.

In standard Bayesian modelling, the prior distribution encodes probabilistic information before observing the data. Its specification affects not only where the posterior is pulled, but also how strongly the prior contributes to posterior regularisation.

The SoU framework adds a separate layer: confidence. Each component of the prior can be paired with a confidence parameter, allowing the researcher to control how strongly that source of uncertainty enters the posterior update. This separates the probabilistic content of a prior component from the degree of confidence assigned to it.

This additional degree of freedom creates a more flexible way to shape posterior behaviour and provides the basis for the sparsity and Bayesian neural network applications below.

## Sources of Uncertainty

It is natural in Bayesian inference to represent uncertainty through subjective probability distributions. It is also natural that the researcher may have different degrees of confidence in different parts of this probabilistic specification.

The **Sources of Uncertainty** framework formalizes this idea by allowing each component of a factorized prior to be paired with a confidence parameter. In this way, the researcher specifies not only prior beliefs, but also how much confidence she assigns to each source of uncertainty.

This adds a new modelling lever to Bayesian inference. Rather than changing only the prior distribution itself, the researcher can also control how strongly each prior component enters the posterior update. This additional flexibility provides the basis for the sparsity and Bayesian neural network applications below.

## Sources of Uncertainty

Bayesian inference represents uncertainty through subjective probability distributions. The **Sources of Uncertainty** framework starts from the observation that the researcher may have different degrees of confidence in different parts of this probabilistic specification.

The framework formalizes this idea by pairing each component of a factorized prior with a confidence parameter. This allows the researcher to specify not only prior beliefs, but also how much confidence she assigns to each source of uncertainty.

This additional modelling lever gives more flexibility in shaping the posterior and motivates the sparsity and Bayesian neural network applications below.

The confidence mechanism is distinct from standard prior specification. While the prior encodes probabilistic information about each component, the confidence parameter controls how strongly that component constrains the posterior update. Separating these two roles gives the researcher an additional modelling lever for shaping posterior concentration and regularisation.

This distinction separates prior informativeness from confidence. Prior informativeness controls how strongly the posterior is pulled toward the prior specification. Confidence, in contrast, provides an additional mechanism for controlling posterior concentration and regularisation. This gives the researcher a new modelling lever for shaping the posterior without changing only the prior distribution itself.

## Sparse Bayesian learning

Building on the Sources of Uncertainty framework, I study sparsity-inducing Bayesian methods based on global-local prior structures.

This leads to **SoU-SGL**, a sparse global-local estimator designed to recover sparse representations rather than merely shrink parameters toward zero.


## Bayesian neural networks

I am also interested in Bayesian deep learning, especially methods that allow neural networks to adapt their effective architecture to the data.

Recent work applies the SoU framework to Bayesian neural networks, where it induces self-pruning and can lead to compact architectures without sacrificing predictive performance.


In current work on convolutional neural networks, the procedure identifies compact architectures with similar total size and layer-wise allocation across different initial widths. They also maintain competitive accuracy with standard neural networks while improving probabilistic performance, including calibration and negative log-likelihood.

## Bayesian neural networks

I apply these ideas to Bayesian neural networks, where structured sparsity can be used to recover compact architectures from overparameterized models.

In current work on convolutional neural networks, the procedure identifies compact architectures with similar total size and layer-wise allocation across different initial widths. These recovered architectures are substantially smaller than the overparameterized deterministic models while maintaining competitive accuracy and improving probabilistic performance, including calibration and negative log-likelihood.

## Bayesian neural networks

I apply **SoU-SGL** to Bayesian neural networks as a mechanism for structured sparsity and self-pruning during training.

In current work, this leads to **SoU-RHS**, a Bayesian structured-sparsity procedure for recovering compact architectures from overparameterized convolutional neural networks. Empirically, the method recovers architectures with similar total size and layer-wise allocation across different starting widths, while maintaining competitive predictive performance and improving probabilistic metrics such as calibration and negative log-likelihood.

## Bayesian neural networks

I apply **SoU-SGL** to Bayesian neural networks as a mechanism for self-pruning during training.

Starting from overparameterized architectures, the method prunes redundant units through the sparsity induced by source-specific confidence. Empirically, this leads to compact architectures with competitive predictive performance.

## Bayesian neural networks

I apply **SoU-SGL** to Bayesian neural networks as a mechanism for self-pruning during training.

The method starts from overparameterized architectures and uses the sparsity induced by source-specific confidence to remove redundant units. In this way, it can robustly recover compact architectures while maintaining competitive predictive performance.
